note: One entry per clip. 'segments' is the narration: one line per on-screen caption, in the order the captions appear in the scene.

segments.caption: A sepsis model running in hundreds of hospitals, scored every 15 minutes.
segments.text: The Epic Sepsis Model ships with a widely used health record and runs at hundreds of US hospitals. It scores every adult inpatient every fifteen minutes and alerts when that score crosses a threshold. Its vendor reported an A U C between zero point seven six and zero point eight three.

segments.caption: Wong et al. validated it on 38,455 hospitalizations at one health system.
segments.text: Wong and colleagues validated it at Michigan Medicine: twenty-seven thousand six hundred ninety-seven patients and thirty-eight thousand four hundred fifty-five hospitalizations, of which two thousand five hundred fifty-two, or seven percent, had sepsis.

segments.caption: The AUC was 0.63, well below the 0.76 to 0.83 the vendor reported.
segments.text: The A U C was zero point six three, with a ninety-five percent interval from zero point six two to zero point six four. The authors also report per-horizon A U Cs of zero point seven two to zero point seven six, then explain why those are misleading: the predictions are not independent of each other.

segments.caption: At the recommended threshold it missed two thirds of sepsis and alerted on 18%.
segments.text: At the vendor's threshold of six, sensitivity was thirty-three percent, so two thirds of sepsis cases were never flagged. The positive predictive value was twelve percent. Alerts fired on eighteen percent of all hospitalizations: eight patients to evaluate for every sepsis case.

segments.caption: The question is not what the model scored, but what the alert added.
segments.text: Now ask what the alert added. Of the two thousand five hundred fifty-two sepsis cases, eight hundred forty-three were flagged, and of those only one hundred eighty-three had not already received timely antibiotics. Of the one thousand seven hundred nine that were missed, one thousand and thirty were treated in time anyway.

segments.caption: Validate locally, and measure what the alert adds to current practice.
segments.text: Two lessons. Validate locally before deployment, because a vendor's A U C came from a vendor's population, not yours. And measure the increment over current practice, not the model on its own. A model is worth deploying only if it changes what happens to a patient.

segments.caption: Once the model is fixed, the threshold is the decision you still make.
segments.text: Once the model is trained, one decision is left: where to put the threshold. These two curves are drawn to the same height, but sepsis is only seven percent of patients, so the red one is really much smaller. Moving the line trades missed cases against false alarms.

segments.caption: At 7% prevalence, three thresholds give very different alert loads.
segments.text: At seven percent prevalence, sensitivity of eighty percent with a positive predictive value of ten percent means fifty-six alerts for every hundred admissions. Fifty percent with twenty percent means seventeen and a half. Twenty-five percent with thirty-five percent means five.

segments.caption: The honest unit is patients reviewed per true case.
segments.text: The honest unit is how many patients a clinician reviews for each real case: ten, five, and about three at those three points. The real sepsis model sat at eight, and it alerted on eighteen percent of all hospitalizations.

segments.caption: And none of it holds still: the inputs change underneath you.
segments.text: None of this holds still. A lab changes an assay, a diagnosis moves to a new code, a unit reopens and the case mix shifts. None of these generates a ticket. The model keeps producing scores that look plausible while the performance moves.

segments.caption: So watch it: a control chart turns drift into something you can see.
segments.text: So watch it. Plot the monthly A U C against limits set from a period you agree was stable. Here it drifts below the lower limit and stays there for three months, which is a signal rather than a bad month.

segments.caption: Write the monitoring plan before go-live, not after the first surprise.
segments.text: Write the plan before go-live. Track inputs, outputs and outcomes. Set the limits in advance. Name the person who is paged when one is crossed, and decide now whether the answer is to retrain, retune, or switch it off.

segments.caption: Put a clinician and a model together and there are two obvious rules.
segments.text: Put a clinician and a model together and there are two obvious rules: flag if either flags, or flag only if both do. Say the clinician catches eighty percent of cases and the model seventy-five. Which rule is better depends on something nobody measures.

segments.caption: Assume their errors are independent, and either-flags reaches 0.95.
segments.text: Assume their errors are independent. Of a hundred real cases, both catch sixty, the clinician alone twenty, the model alone fifteen, and five are missed by both. Either-flags reaches zero point nine five, and both-flags falls to zero point six zero.

segments.caption: Assume the clinician's misses are a subset of the model's, and both numbers flip.
segments.text: Now assume the model misses whatever the clinician misses. Both catch seventy-five, the clinician alone five, and twenty are missed by both. Either-flags falls to zero point eight zero, which is the clinician alone, so the model adds nothing. Both-flags rises to zero point seven five. The same two sensitivities, opposite conclusions.

segments.caption: And people are not rules: the combination has to be measured.
segments.text: And people are not rules. A confident score can talk a clinician out of a correct judgement, and at one true case in every eight alerts the rational response is to stop reading them. Goh and colleagues measured exactly this: the model alone scored ninety-two percent, and the physicians using it scored seventy-six, against seventy-four without.

segments.caption: Ambient intelligence watches the room instead of waiting to be told.
segments.text: Ambient intelligence watches the room instead of waiting for someone to type. Sixteen depth sensors detected hand hygiene at ninety-two point one percent sensitivity, better than the human observers at eighty-five point two. But that came from only eighty-eight events, so read the interval. In an I C U, seven sensors detected mobility at eighty-seven percent, and counted the staff involved correctly only sixty-nine percent of the time.

segments.caption: Sensing a care space is a governance question before it is a technical one.
segments.text: Sensing a care space is a governance question first. Depth sensing keeps identifiable images out of the room, which helps, but it does not settle who consents, who sees the data, or how long it is kept, and the staff are being observed too. Validate locally, watch it after go-live, and measure the team rather than the model.
